tour.title: Shanghai – The Bund & Old Town
tour.summary: Treaty-port Shanghai in one walk: the Bund's banking palaces, a steel bridge over the creek, neon Nanjing Road, a Ming garden, dumplings by a zigzag bridge, and the lane streets of Tianzifang.
tour.overviewText:
Stand on the river wall at nine in the morning, trams of tourists behind you and the future glaring at you from across the water, and you are standing inside the deal that made modern China argue with itself. This walk is your way through it.

Shanghai matters because for a century it was China's forced open door. After Britain defeated China in the First Opium War — fought over Britain's opium trade — the 1842 Treaty of Nanking forced open five ports, Shanghai among them, and foreigners carved out self-governed concessions, slices of the city ruled by foreign powers, along this riverbank. British, American and French traders built banks and clubs on the Bund — the waitan, meaning the outer bank — while millions of Chinese migrants built the tenements behind them, and the money piled up on both sides until war ended it: the Japanese occupied the city in 1937, and the Communist victory of 1949 closed the century of foreign rule. Supporters of the old order called it free trade and modernity; Chinese histories call it national humiliation; the stones hold both, and this tour states them and moves on. What rose from the same mud is the engine you see across the river: Lujiazui, the finance district of towers — the 632-metre Shanghai Tower, the bottle-opener Jin Mao — where the reopened stock exchange and half the world's banks price China's money. The port grew rich on trade and stayed rich on finance.

The people around you are two cities at once. Shanghainese — the local Wu-dialect speech, fast, sly, proud — belongs to families who queue for soup dumplings and argue about school districts; Mandarin belongs to the newcomers from every province who pour the concrete and code the apps. Daily life runs on breakfast Shengjian and metro Line 2, on aunties dancing in plazas at dawn and couriers napping on scooters at noon. Outsiders get Shanghai wrong by calling it the least Chinese city in China, a skyline with no soul. Walk the old town lanes behind the neon and you will see the error: the commerce is global, but the appetites, the superstitions and the gossip are Chinese to the core.

The shape of the walk is a river morning and an old-town afternoon. You start on the Bund promenade, look north from the steel bridge, cut inland through the Nanjing Road crowds, then ride south to the Ming garden, the temple and the teahouse pond, ending in the lanes of Tianzifang.

Late December is Shanghai at its greyest: damp, 3 to 8 degrees, a wind off the river that finds every gap, dusk falling before 17:00. Wear the warm coat and bring gloves; the heated metro is your refuge between acts. Money is RMB, meaning yuan, the Chinese currency also written CNY — phones pay for nearly everything, but keep small notes for dumpling stalls and temple incense. Start around 09:00 with an empty stomach; the dumplings are not optional.

Eat first, judge later. Old Shanghai rewards the hungry.
tour.difficulty: Easy. About 3.5 km of flat walking plus one metro ride; the difficulty is density, not distance — dense crowds on the Bund, Nanjing Road and around Yu Garden, steps and thresholds in the garden and temple, and narrow uneven lanes at Tianzifang.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 09:00. In mid-to-late December the light is thin and the wind is sharp, so do the Bund in the morning, take the garden and temple at midday when queues shorten, and reach Tianzifang by mid-afternoon before the early dusk.

stops.name: The Bund Promenade
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open promenade along the Huangpu. No ticket and no gate; verify locally only if arriving very late, when sections near construction may be fenced.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily. Best in morning light; the crowds thicken from late morning and the buildings light up after dark.
stops.accessibility: Wide, flat, paved promenade, step free along its length. Crowds are dense at weekends; the flood wall steps down to the river are steep and unrailed.
stops.insiderTip: Read the buildings west to east, not the skyline: the domes, clocks and carved banking halls are the museum, and the towers across the water are merely the gift shop.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north along the promenade about 320 metres, roughly 5 minutes, toward the steel bridge where the creek meets the river. The red truss ahead is the next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: LosAngelesT, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Walk out onto the raised promenade and turn around: the money faces the water. Behind you runs a mile of domes, clocks and carved stone — the banks and clubs of treaty-port Shanghai — and across the grey river the towers of Pudong answer back like a younger sibling shouting. You are on the Bund, the waitan, meaning the outer bank: the embankment road foreigners laid along the Huangpu after Shanghai was forced open to foreign trade in 1842.

The building type around you is the lesson. A concession was a slice of a Chinese city governed by foreigners, and here Britain and America ran their International Settlement while France ran its own district to the south. So the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank raised a domed palazzo at No. 12, the Customs House raised a clock tower at No. 13, and Sassoon's Cathay Hotel — today's Peace Hotel, the green-pyramid art deco block at the Nanjing Road corner — poured jazz over it all from 1929. Chinese merchants and bankers worked these same rooms as compradors and clerks, learning the trade that would later build Pudong. Foreign capital, Chinese labour, one river wall.

Read it the way the tour asks you to hold two thoughts. The architecture is genuinely grand, and it is also the footprint of an unequal deal, built while millions crowded into tenements a few streets inland. Both are true, and neither needs your verdict. Prices here are in RMB, meaning yuan (CNY) — the dumpling stalls take small notes, the hotel bars take your whole wallet.

No ticket, open promenade, flat and step free but crowded. When the wind off the river finds your collar, walk north about 320 metres, roughly 5 minutes, toward the red steel bridge. That is your next stop.

stops.name: Waibaidu Bridge Viewpoint
stops.entranceFeeNote: Public road bridge with pedestrian walkways. No ticket; verify locally as walkway sections occasionally close for works.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily. The viewpoint from the promenade end is best in morning light, before the traffic thickens.
stops.accessibility: Flat promenade approach, step free. The bridge walkways are narrow with traffic close beside you; wheelchair users may prefer the view from the promenade end.
stops.insiderTip: Stand at the promenade end and look west up the creek, not just at the truss: the old warehouses and new galleries of the north bank are where the city's art scene quietly moved.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn back south along the promenade, then cut inland at Nanjing Road. Walk about 1.0 km, roughly 15 minutes, west along the pedestrian street to the bright canyon of shopfronts. The crowds thicken as you go.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Kallerna, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Follow the promenade north until the river wall ends at a red steel truss. This is Waibaidu Bridge — the Garden Bridge, as the foreigners called it — thrown across Suzhou Creek where the creek joins the Huangpu, and completed in 1907 as one of China's first all-steel bridges.

The mechanism is a border drawn in iron. The creek was the line between the British-run settlement on this side and the Chinese-administered districts beyond, and for decades this bridge was the gate between them: rickshaws, refugees, soldiers and spies all crossed it, and in 1937 the guns of the battle for Shanghai crossed it too. Stand at the promenade end and look at the rivets. Every plate was shipped in, bolted by hand, and painted the red-brown you see today — a bridge built to carry empire traffic that ended up carrying everyone's commute.

Look west up the creek while you are here. The old warehouses on the far bank now hold galleries and bookshops; the art scene moved where the rent was cheap, which is the oldest Shanghai story there is.

No ticket, narrow walkways, traffic close beside you. When you have your photograph, turn back south along the promenade and cut inland at Nanjing Road: about 1.0 km, roughly 15 minutes, into the bright canyon of shopfronts.

stops.name: Nanjing Road Pedestrian Street
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open pedestrian street. No ticket; shops and snack stalls price in RMB (CNY). Verify food prices as you go — the street is honest but tourist-priced at the eastern end.
stops.openingHours: Open access daily. Shops roughly 10:00 to 22:00; the street is liveliest from late morning, and jostling by afternoon.
stops.accessibility: Flat, wide, paved and step free along its length. Crowds are extremely dense at weekends and holidays; mornings are the calm window.
stops.insiderTip: Look above the ground floors: the department-store facades of Wing On and Sincere still carry the names of the Chinese firms that taught this street to outsell the foreign shops a century ago.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south from the pedestrian street about 1.7 km, roughly 25 minutes, via Henan and Fuyou Roads toward the old town. The shopfronts shrink, the lanes narrow, and the grey-tiled roofs ahead mean the garden district.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Hermann Luyken, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Turn inland off the Bund and the street swallows you whole. This is Nanjing Road East, China's most famous shopping street, a pedestrian river of neon, dumpling steam and a million footsteps a day — and it has been selling things on this exact line since the 1850s, when it was Nanking Road in the foreign settlement.

The mechanism is imitation in reverse. Foreign department stores taught Shanghai window shopping; then Chinese firms — Wing On, Sincere, the names still on the facades above you — outsold them by understanding local tastes, instalment credit and festival hunger. The street you are jostling through is the victory lap of Chinese retail over its teachers. Browsing is free, prices in RMB (yuan), and the snack windows halfway down are your second breakfast: shengjianbao, those pan-fried pork buns with the crisp bottoms, eaten standing like a local.

Flat and step free, but this is the densest crowd of your day — keep valuables zipped and children in sight. When you have eaten, walk south about 1.7 km, roughly 25 minutes, via Henan and Fuyou Roads. The towers thin, the lanes narrow, and the grey tiles ahead mean the old town.

stops.name: Yu Garden
stops.entranceFeeNote: Ticketed garden: about ¥30–40 (CNY) at last check, varying by season. Verify prices at the gate; Chinese gardens revise them, and entry is capped at busy times.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly morning to late afternoon with last entry well before closing. Verify locally and arrive before midday to beat the tour groups.
stops.accessibility: Not step free. Narrow moon gates, steep rockery steps, high thresholds and uneven paving throughout; the garden is hard going for wheels and small children must be carried at the rockeries.
stops.insiderTip: Find the Exquisite Jade Rock in its courtyard: a three-metre Taihu stone so perforated it is said a stick of incense lit at the base smokes from every hole at once.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the south gate and walk about 280 metres, roughly 5 minutes, south through the bazaar lanes to the temple courtyard. The smell of incense means you have arrived.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Kallerna, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Duck through the gate out of the neon and the noise drops by half. You are in Yu Garden — Yuyuan, the Garden of Pleasing — a Ming-dynasty private garden begun in 1559 by Pan Yunduan, a Shanghai official, as a retirement gift for his father. The Ming were the Chinese emperors who ruled from the 1300s to the 1600s, before the Qing, the last dynasty, took over.

The mechanism is a whole landscape folded into two hectares. Piled rockeries you can climb, ponds crossed by white bridges, walls ridden by clay dragons, pavilions placed so every doorway frames a different painting of stone and water. Nothing here is natural and everything teaches: the jagged Taihu rocks show endurance, the carp show abundance, the zigzag paths slow you into noticing. Then read the scars. Rebels of the Small Swords Society — a secret brotherhood that seized the old town in 1853 — made this garden their headquarters; foreign troops shelled it; the gardeners rebuilt it anyway. Ticket about ¥30–40, meaning yuan (CNY), verify at the gate.

Blunt warning: this is the least accessible stop of the day — moon gates, rockery steps, thresholds, crowds funnelling through gaps two people wide. Take it slowly, carry small children at the rocks, and leave by the south gate: about 280 metres, roughly 5 minutes, through the bazaar to the temple courtyard.

stops.name: Shanghai Old City God Temple
stops.entranceFeeNote: Ticketed temple courtyard: about ¥10 (CNY) at last check. Incense and fortune sticks cost extra inside. Verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly morning to late afternoon. Verify locally; visiting is restricted during services, and incense smoke is heavy on festival days.
stops.accessibility: High stone thresholds at every hall door and steps between courtyards; the courtyards are level once you are over the sills. Incense smoke is thick — asthmatics should keep to the outer court.
stops.insiderTip: Watch what worshippers do with the fortune sticks, not just the statues: the shake, the numbered fall, the matching slip read at the counter is a 1,000-year-old random-access oracle still in daily use.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north about 210 metres, roughly 3 minutes, back through the bazaar to the pond. The zigzag bridge and the square pavilion in the middle of the water are the next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Livepine, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Follow the incense south through the bazaar and you reach the walled town's guardian. This is the City God Temple — Chenghuangmiao — a Taoist temple raised in the Ming dynasty to Qin Yubo, a local official honoured after death as Shanghai's protective deity. Taoism is China's native religion of the Way, of gods and immortals, incense and fortune-telling, and a City God is exactly what it says: the divine magistrate of one walled town, prayed to for exam passes, safe voyages and fair verdicts.

The mechanism is bureaucracy mirrored in heaven. Worshippers address the god the way they would an official: petition, offering, patience. Shake the cylinder of fortune sticks until one jumps out, take its number to the counter, and receive a printed slip of classical verse to decode your question — marriage, business, health. Entry runs about ¥10 (yuan), verify at the gate; incense costs extra and the smoke is genuinely thick on busy days. Mind the high thresholds at every hall door, and keep your voice down near anyone praying — this is a working temple, not a set.

When you leave, walk north about 210 metres, roughly 3 minutes, back to the pond. The zigzag bridge and the pavilion in the middle of the water are your lunch.

stops.name: Huxinting Teahouse & Jiuqu Bridge
stops.entranceFeeNote: The bridge and pond are free to cross and photograph. Tea in the pavilion runs from about ¥30 (CNY) a pot at last check. Verify prices; the dumpling house next door queues separately.
stops.openingHours: Pond area open daily in daylight. The teahouse keeps roughly 09:00 to 21:00 hours; verify locally as times shift by season.
stops.accessibility: The zigzag bridge has steps at each turn and no railings in places; the pavilion interior is tight. The pond can be fully enjoyed step free from the shore railings.
stops.insiderTip: Order the cheapest pot and the window seat, not the ceremony: the view down the zigzag bridge with the old roofs behind it is what you are paying for, and it costs the same in every grade of tea.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is the metro hop, not a walk: Tianzifang is 4.0 km south west — about an hour on foot through heavy traffic — so do not stroll it. Walk 10 minutes to Yuyuan Station, ride Line 10 one stop to Laoximen, change to Line 8 one stop to Lujiabang Road, then walk 15 minutes west to Taikang Road. Allow about 35 minutes door to door.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: KimonBerlin, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Cross the water by the bridge that refuses to go straight. Jiuqu — the Nine-Bend Bridge — zigzags across the pond to the square pavilion in the middle, and they say it bends so evil spirits, which can only travel in straight lines, cannot follow you across. Whether or not you buy the demonology, buy the engineering: every turn is a new framed view of roofs, crowds and sky.

The pavilion is Huxinting, the Pavilion in the Lake, a teahouse that has poured here since the 1850s — one of the oldest in Shanghai. A pot from about ¥30 (yuan), verify prices, buys you a window seat over the water and twenty unhurried minutes. And beside the pond, at the century-old Nanxiang dumpling house, queues form for the city's most famous xiaolongbao — soup dumplings, meaning thin-skinned pork parcels with hot broth sealed inside, invented in the Shanghai suburb of Nanxiang. Nibble a corner, sip the soup, then eat with vinegar and ginger, standing like everyone else.

The bridge steps turn tightly with patchy railings; the shore railings give the full view step free. When the tea is done, do not walk south. Tianzifang is 4.0 km away, about an hour on foot through heavy traffic. Walk 10 minutes to Yuyuan Station, ride Line 10 one stop to Laoximen, change to Line 8 one stop to Lujiabang Road, then walk 15 minutes west to Taikang Road. Allow about 35 minutes door to door.

stops.name: Tianzifang Lanes
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open lanes; browsing is free. Studios and snack stalls price in RMB (CNY); haggle politely and compare two stalls before buying art.
stops.openingHours: Lanes open access daily. Shops roughly 10:00 to 22:00; late afternoon is the sweet spot, before the bar crowds arrive.
stops.accessibility: Narrow lanes, uneven stones, steps and thresholds everywhere; not step free and hard going for wheels. The crowds peak on weekend afternoons.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the laundry lines and the lunch tables, not just the galleries: residents still live above the shops, and the lanes that kept their tenants are the ones that kept their soul.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Retrace the lanes to the Taikang Road entrance, where taxis wait; Dapuqiao metro station (Line 9) is about 10 minutes on foot. The plane-tree streets of the former French Concession begin just west of here and wait for their own tour.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: 钉钉, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
stops.narration:
Come up out of the metro and the city exhales into brick and laundry lines. This is Tianzifang, a warren of 1930s lilong lanes at 210 Taikang Road — lilong meaning lane neighbourhoods, and their stone-gated houses called shikumen, stone-warehouse-gate, after the carved doorframes every family passed through.

The mechanism is rescue by tenancy. Developers pencilled these lanes for demolition; from the late 1990s artists rented the empty workshops instead, a painter's studio became a street of galleries, and the residents who stayed upstairs kept it a neighbourhood instead of a stage set. Browsing is free, prices in yuan, and the workshops sell what they make: prints, ceramics, silk, tea. Compare it in your head with Xintiandi, the glossy rebuilt lanes east of here — developer money versus tenant stubbornness — and notice which one still hangs its washing out.

Narrow stones, steps, thresholds, weekend crowds: not step free, and December dusk comes early, so keep your footing. End of the walk. You started where foreign banks faced down the river, and you finish where lane families faced down the bulldozers — same city, same stubbornness, a century apart. The plane-tree streets of the old French district begin just west of here, and they get their own tour. Go eat something — you have earned it.
